description: Agent-readable reference for common mathematical notation. Models check definitions in the statement, proof, cited predecessors and glossary_introduces themselves. Explicit local definitions and hypotheses determine the meaning; aliases are contextual, not unconditional equivalences. This reference does not supply verified facts or automatically certify symbol coverage. See DATA_MODEL.md.

Z>=k.definition: The set of integers >= k, i.e. {k, k+1, k+2, ...}; concrete k must be substituted at the point of use (Z>=0 = nonnegative integers, Z>=2, etc.).

N.definition: The natural numbers. Convention: N starts at 0 unless restated locally; use Z+ for {1,2,3,...} when 1-based is required.

R+.definition: The set of strictly positive real numbers, i.e. {x in R : x > 0}.

R>=0.definition: The set of nonnegative real numbers, i.e. {x in R : x >= 0}.

floor(x).definition: For x in R, floor(x) is the unique integer n with n <= x < n+1.
aliases: [x] (when context is integer part, but prefer floor)

ceil(x).definition: For x in R, ceil(x) is the unique integer n with n-1 < x <= n.

{x}.definition: In fractional-part notation, for x in R, {x} = x - floor(x), the unique element of [0,1) congruent to x mod 1. In set notation, {x} instead denotes the singleton containing x; disambiguate by context or write frac(x).

gcd.definition: gcd(a, b) is the greatest common divisor of integers a, b (with gcd(0, 0) = 0 by convention).

lcm.definition: lcm(a, b) is the least common multiple of integers a, b (with lcm(a, 0) = 0).

mod.definition: a mod b (for b != 0) is the unique nonnegative integer r with 0 <= r < |b| and a = qb + r for some integer q.

divides.definition: For integers a, b, 'a divides b' (a | b) means there exists an integer k with b = ka.

[a,b].definition: Closed real interval {x in R : a <= x <= b}. When a, b are integers and the integer interval is meant, restate explicitly as 'integer interval' or use {a, a+1, ..., b}.

(a,b).definition: In interval notation, the open real interval {x in R : a < x < b}. The same parentheses can denote an ordered pair in other contexts; state which meaning is intended.

[a,b).definition: Half-open real interval {x in R : a <= x < b}.

(a,b].definition: Half-open real interval {x in R : a < x <= b}.

iff.definition: If and only if; logical biconditional.

sgn(x).definition: Sign function: sgn(x) = 1 if x > 0, 0 if x = 0, -1 if x < 0.

epsilon.definition: Conventional name for a small real parameter; introduce with an explicit range, e.g. 'let epsilon in (0, 1/Q)'.

eta.definition: Two standard meanings, disambiguated by context: (i) a small positive real parameter (use with explicit range like 'eta in R+, eta < ...'); (ii) the generic point of an integral scheme.

delta.definition: Conventional name for a (small or fixed) real parameter; introduce with an explicit value or range (e.g. 'put delta := deg_C(f^* T_{X/B}) > 0').

lambda.definition: Conventional name for a real or complex parameter / scalar / eigenvalue; introduce with an explicit type (e.g. 'lambda in R+', 'lambda an eigenvalue of A').

mu.definition: Standard meanings include (i) the slope mu(E) := deg(E)/rk(E) of a coherent sheaf on a curve; (ii) a real parameter (introduce with range). Disambiguate by context at the point of use.

nu.definition: Conventional name for a finite covering morphism (e.g. nu : B -> C of degree e), or for a normalization morphism, or sometimes for a real parameter; introduce with the specific role at point of use.

rho.definition: Conventional name for a structure morphism, projection, or scheme map (e.g. rho : W -> B). Introduce the source, target, and any extra structure (projective, dominant, smooth, ...) at the point of use.

sigma.definition: Conventional name for a section of a morphism (e.g. sigma : B -> W is a section of rho : W -> B), or sometimes for a permutation. Introduce the role and source/target at the point of use.

phi.definition: Conventional name for a morphism between schemes / varieties (e.g. phi : W -> X). Introduce source, target, and any further structure at the point of use.

pi.definition: Two standard meanings, disambiguated by context: (i) a structural morphism (e.g. pi : X -> B is a projection or projective morphism); (ii) Archimedes' constant pi = 3.14... in analysis. Introduce the role at the point of use.

tau.definition: Conventional name for a stabilization morphism (Kontsevich), a transposition / permutation, or another auxiliary map. Introduce the role at the point of use.

Phi.definition: Capital phi; conventional name for a Frobenius-type morphism (e.g. geometric Frobenius Phi_m : C_m -> C of degree p^m), or a more general system of morphisms. Introduce the role at the point of use.

Pi.definition: Capital pi; conventional name for a product (Pi_{i in I} a_i), a projection, or another structural map / scheme. Disambiguate at the point of use.

Sigma.definition: Capital sigma; conventional name for a sum, a set, or in algebraic geometry an irreducible curve in a variety (often a rational curve produced by bend-and-break). Disambiguate at the point of use.

Gamma.definition: Capital gamma; conventional name for a graph (e.g. dual graph of a nodal curve), a curve, or a discrete group. Disambiguate at the point of use.

chi.definition: Euler characteristic: for a coherent sheaf F on a projective scheme Y, chi(Y, F) := sum_i (-1)^i h^i(Y, F). On a smooth projective curve C of genus g, chi(C, E) = deg E + rk(E)(1 - g) for a vector bundle E (Riemann-Roch).

h^i.definition: Sheaf cohomology dimension: h^i(Y, F) := dim_k H^i(Y, F) for a coherent sheaf F on a projective k-scheme Y.

X_b.definition: Schematic fiber of a morphism rho : X -> B over a point b in B; defined as X x_B Spec(k(b)) (or X x_B {b} when b is a closed point of B).

O_{Y,y}.definition: Local ring of a scheme Y at a point y; the stalk of the structure sheaf O_Y at y. For a smooth curve B and a closed point b in B, O_{B,b} is a DVR.

T_Y.definition: Tangent sheaf of a scheme Y; on the smooth locus it is a vector bundle of rank dim Y. For a morphism Y -> Z it makes sense to talk about the relative tangent T_{Y/Z}.

T_{Y/Z}.definition: Relative tangent sheaf for a morphism Y -> Z; on the smooth locus of the morphism it is a vector bundle of rank dim Y - dim Z.

forall.definition: Universal quantifier: forall x in A, P(x) asserts that P(x) holds for every element of A. State the domain and scope of each quantifier; quantifier order matters.

exists.definition: Existential quantifier: exists x in A such that P(x) asserts that at least one such element exists. The notation exists! asserts existence of exactly one such element.

implies.definition: Logical implication P => Q: if P holds, then Q holds. It does not assert the converse Q => P or assert P on its own.

emptyset.definition: The empty set, containing no elements. It differs from {0} and from {emptyset}, each of which has one element.

x in A.definition: Set membership: x is an element of A. Membership is distinct from the subset relation between two sets.

A subseteq B.definition: Every element of A is an element of B; equality A = B is allowed. The unqualified symbol subset is used with differing conventions, so state whether equality is permitted.

A subsetneq B.definition: Proper inclusion: A subseteq B and A != B.

A union B.definition: The set of elements belonging to A or B, including those belonging to both. This does not assert that A and B are disjoint.

A intersect B.definition: The set of elements belonging to both A and B.

A setminus B.definition: Set difference: {x in A : x not in B}. A complement A^c means U setminus A only relative to a specified ambient set U.

A x B.definition: Cartesian product: the set of ordered pairs (a,b) with a in A and b in B. Here parentheses denote an ordered pair, not a real interval.

P(A).definition: In set-theoretic notation, the power set of A: the set of all subsets of A. It is also written 2^A. Do not confuse this use of P with a probability measure.

|A|.definition: For a set A, its cardinality; for finite A, the number of its elements. Infinite cardinality requires the relevant set-theoretic interpretation. Vertical bars have other meanings for numbers, matrices and divisibility.

f: A -> B.definition: A function with domain A and codomain B, assigning each a in A exactly one value f(a) in B. This notation alone implies neither injectivity nor surjectivity; the image may be a proper subset of B.

f^{-1}(S).definition: For f: A -> B and S subseteq B, the inverse image {a in A : f(a) in S}. This is defined without assuming f is invertible. An inverse function f^{-1}: B -> A instead requires f to be bijective.

g o f.definition: Composition: for f: A -> B and g: B -> C, (g o f)(a) = g(f(a)). The rightmost function is applied first; domains and codomains must be compatible.

a equiv b (mod m).definition: For integers a, b and positive integer m, a and b are congruent modulo m when m divides a-b. This is a relation, distinct from the operation returning a remainder.

coprime.definition: Integers a and b are coprime when gcd(a,b) = 1. For more than two integers, having collective gcd 1 does not imply pairwise coprimality; specify which condition is intended.

n!.definition: For a nonnegative integer n, n! is the product of the integers from 1 through n, with 0! = 1. Extension outside nonnegative integers is not implicit.

binom(n,k).definition: For integers n >= 0 and 0 <= k <= n, the binomial coefficient n!/(k!(n-k)!), counting k-element subsets of an n-element set. With n >= 0 it is commonly set to 0 for integer k outside this range; state any generalized convention.

span(S).definition: For a subset S of a vector space V over a specified field K, the set of all finite K-linear combinations of elements of S; span(emptyset) = {0}. The scalar field is part of the definition.

ker(T).definition: For a linear map T: V -> W, its kernel {v in V : T(v) = 0_W}. In other algebraic categories, specify the corresponding notion of kernel rather than silently reusing the vector-space definition.

im(T).definition: For a linear map T: V -> W, its image {T(v) : v in V}, a subspace of W. For an arbitrary function, the image is a set, not necessarily a vector space.

dim(V).definition: The dimension of a vector space V over a specified field K: the cardinality of a basis; a nonnegative integer in the finite-dimensional case. Dimensions over different scalar fields need not agree.

rank(T).definition: For a linear map T, rank(T) = dim(im(T)) over the specified scalar field. For a matrix, use its associated linear map over that field; changing the field can change the rank.

det(A).definition: For a square n by n matrix A over a commutative ring, det(A) = sum over permutations sigma of sgn(sigma) times the product of A[i,sigma(i)] for i = 1,...,n. The 0 by 0 determinant is 1 by convention; an ordinary determinant is not defined for a nonsquare matrix.

||v||.definition: A specified norm on a real or complex vector space: nonnegative, zero exactly at v = 0, absolutely homogeneous, and satisfying the triangle inequality. Do not assume the Euclidean, operator or another norm without a stated convention.

<u,v>.definition: In an inner-product space, the specified positive-definite inner product of u and v. Over C it is conjugate-symmetric and linear in one argument, conjugate-linear in the other; state which argument is linear. Angle brackets can also denote a generated subgroup or a dual pairing, which require separate context.

|x|.definition: For real x, its absolute value max(x,-x); for complex z, its modulus sqrt(z times conjugate(z)). These are distinct uses from set cardinality, divisibility, determinants and conditional-probability bars.

sup(A).definition: For a nonempty real set A bounded above, its least upper bound: the smallest real s with a <= s for every a in A. It need not belong to A. State conventions separately when empty sets or extended-real values are allowed.

inf(A).definition: For a nonempty real set A bounded below, its greatest lower bound: the largest real t with t <= a for every a in A. It need not belong to A. State conventions separately when empty sets or extended-real values are allowed.

max(A).definition: A greatest element of an ordered set A: an element M in A such that a <= M for every a in A. A maximum need not exist; a finite real supremum alone does not ensure it is attained.

min(A).definition: A least element of an ordered set A: an element m in A such that m <= a for every a in A. A minimum need not exist; a finite real infimum alone does not ensure it is attained.

log(x).definition: For real x > 0, a logarithm with a specified base b > 0, b != 1. ln(x) denotes base e; bare log commonly means ln in analysis, but the base must be clear. A complex logarithm requires a branch or a multivalued interpretation to be stated.

lim_{x->a} f(x).definition: For a real-valued function on a real domain D and an accumulation point a of D, the finite limit L means: for every epsilon > 0 there exists delta > 0 such that x in D and 0 < |x-a| < delta imply |f(x)-L| < epsilon. State one-sided, infinite or other topological limit conventions explicitly.

O(g).definition: In a stated limiting regime, f = O(g) means |f| <= C|g| throughout some neighborhood or eventual range, for a fixed C > 0. Specify which parameters C and the range may depend on; uniformity in extra parameters is not automatic.

o(g).definition: In a stated limiting regime, f = o(g) means that for every epsilon > 0, eventually |f| <= epsilon|g|. Where g is eventually nonzero, this is equivalent to f/g -> 0. Specify any uniformity in extra parameters.

Pr(E).definition: The probability of a measurable event E under a specified probability measure on a specified probability space. A conditioning expression Pr(E | F) with an event F requires Pr(F) > 0 for the elementary ratio definition.

E[X].definition: On a specified probability space, the expectation of an integrable real random variable X is its integral with respect to the probability measure. For nonnegative X, the extended expectation may equal +infinity; arbitrary nonintegrable signed variables need not have a defined expectation.
